fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. Neco, king of Egypt, marches up to fight at Carchemish, and "…Josiah went out to confront him." A king comes marching up, and Josiah goes out to meet him. I'd have stayed home and checked on my ovens.

I like the peaceful picture, baker, but that's not what the text says. It says "…Josiah went out to confront him." He went out to confront Neco, king of Egypt, not to stay put and pray. Going out is what the text shows.

Yes, baker! Neco sent messengers to Josiah, saying, "I have not come against you today, but I am fighting another dynasty…" So the message was that Neco's fight was with another dynasty. Josiah was told this before anything else happened.

Close, but the text says otherwise, baker. Neco's messengers tell Josiah, "I have not come against you today, but I am fighting another dynasty…" So Neco says he has not come against Josiah today. His message was that he was fighting another dynasty.

Not quite, friend. Neco never says anything about turning back. He says he's fighting another dynasty and that "…God has told me to hurry." Hurry is the instruction he names, and it isn't turning back home.
Good guess, since Carchemish is by the Euphrates, baker. But Neco says nothing about waiting. He says, "…God has told me to hurry." Hurry is the word he uses, not wait.

Not quite, baker. After the warning, "Josiah, however, did not turn away from him…" That "however" tells you which way it went. The text says he did not listen to Neco's words and went to fight him on the Plain of Megiddo.

You got it, baker. The text says Josiah "…did not listen to Neco’s words from the mouth of God…" So the words Neco spoke were from the mouth of God. Josiah did not listen, and he went to fight on the Plain of Megiddo.
Carchemish is where Neco marched up to fight, baker, not where Josiah died. The text says his servants "…brought him to Jerusalem, where he died." The archers shot Josiah on the Plain of Megiddo.
Good guess, baker, but the word is "statute." The text says they "…established them as a statute for Israel…" A statute is a set rule, not a sign. So the laments became a set rule for Israel.

The Book of the Wars of the LORD shows up in Numbers 21:14, friend, but this passage names a different book. Josiah's acts "…are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah." That's the book to remember here.
